prize_parts.citation: for the development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: After reading the full first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: B052 as a single part for Buchwald and Hartwig. The scientific case rests on what was actually solved. Forming an aryl C-N bond with palladium required controlling C-N reductive elimination from a Pd-amide and suppressing beta-hydride elimination and catalyst deactivation, and that was achieved by ligand design (bulky biaryl and hindered alkyl phosphines) and by mechanistic work on oxidative addition, amine binding and reductive elimination. This is a distinct problem from the C-C couplings honoured in 2010, not a change of substrate. The method has three decades of independent confirmation and is routine in pharmaceutical, agrochemical and organic-materials synthesis. Exact credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, because two groups independently built general, ligand-controlled catalysts. Four members, including me, put it in their preferred configuration, and every one of them names exactly Buchwald and Hartwig. I give that agreement little weight on its own. The case holds because the principle, the maturity and the attribution each stand up without it. I considered Aili's two-part pairing with B004 and decided against it, for the reasons given in my responses.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still that the committee may read B052 as a sequel to the 2010 prize, so that its conceptual novelty is judged lower than that of phase separation or base editing. Kosugi's earlier tin-amide coupling remains a real precursor. The chair asks which documents settle it, and I cannot cite one: the files do not contain a primary-source comparison, and my 1994-1995 timeline is recollection. My position that his reaction was limited in scope and not ligand-controlled is a judgment from memory and should be checked against the original papers before any citation wording is fixed. I also accept that my ranking favours enabling methods, which is a bias of my own field, and that a purely synthetic prize leaves biology-facing and physical-chemistry achievements unrecognised this year.

responses.point: A two-part prize pairing B052 (Buchwald, Hartwig) with B004 (Liu alone) would balance a mature synthetic method with a newer biomolecular tool and fits the three-laureate limit as two plus one.
responses.response: I take the balance argument seriously and I agree on the chemistry of both parts, but I do not support the pairing. The allocation works only by crediting Liu alone, and you yourself say that omits Komor and Gaudelli, whose first-author work defined the cytosine and adenine editors, and Target-AID is an independent line. Adding B004 would put its unresolved attribution and its closeness to the 2020 CRISPR prize into a prize that is otherwise clean. B052 is complete as one part, and I do not think a prize needs a second part for variety. If the committee insists on two parts, B004 is my first alternative, but only once the credit question is settled on evidence about who conceived each editor class.

responses.point: Phase separation (B002) gives one quantitative physical-chemical principle, with the 2009 P-granule demonstration and Rosen's 2012 multivalent reconstitution as concrete foundations, and is textbook-level after fifteen years.
responses.response: The 2012 in vitro reconstitution with defined multivalent proteins is the strongest evidence for the principle, and it persuades me that the phenomenon is real as chemistry. That is why B002 is now my second alternative. My remaining doubt is the one you list: which cellular condensates are liquid and functional in vivo, as opposed to products of overexpression and imaging, is not settled for most examples, and a citation has to state a discovery without that qualifier. The names also stay open. Pappu and Mittag supplied the sticker-spacer theory, so a three-name set splits the credit between the in vivo discovery and the theory. B052 has neither problem. I would not rank B002 above it today, but I would support revisiting it in a later year as the in vivo evidence matures.

responses.point: B002 introduced a new concept of molecular organisation, and physical chemistry has had little recognition compared with synthesis in recent years.
responses.response: I agree that physical chemistry deserves recognition, and this is the most persuasive argument for B002. It is a point about balance across years, though, not about the merit of this year's candidates. You also say that some of the field's claims are probably overstated, and I think a prize committee should wait until the validated claims have been separated from those. I read your own caution as an argument for patience on B002, not against B052. Your listing of B052 as an alternative suggests we agree that its attribution and impact are secure.

responses.point: Base editing (B004) is a clean chemical-mechanism story, with directed evolution of an adenine deaminase for DNA, and Liu, Komor and Gaudelli would be the right set, though Kondo and Nishida's Target-AID is an open credit question.
responses.response: I accept your point that the adenine editor is new chemistry, since a deaminase with no natural DNA substrate had to be evolved, and I keep B004 as an alternative on that basis. What keeps it below B052 for me is credit and timing together. The cap of three cannot separate Liu, Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida without a judgment on conception that the files do not support, and you note yourself that Liu's laboratory also stands behind prime editing, so the boundary of the credited discovery is unclear. Clinical durability and off-target data are still accumulating. I would expect B004 to be stronger in a few years, whereas B052 will not change.

responses.point: The strongest objection to B052 is that it reads as an extension of the 2010 prize, and Kosugi and Migita-type precursors raise a priority question that cannot be settled from the files.
responses.response: We state the objection in the same terms. My answer is about mechanism: C-N bond formation needed ligand control of reductive elimination from a palladium-amide, which was not a feature of the C-C couplings honoured in 2010. On Kosugi, I agree that we cannot settle priority from the files. What we can do is word the citation as 'development of palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling', which makes no first-ever claim, and mention the precursor in the committee's background report, with the original papers verified. I would also keep the citation free of C-H functionalisation, as you suggest, so that Hartwig's other candidate is not implied.

responses.point: Long-range electron transfer through proteins (B009) is a quantitative mechanism with a clean two-person attribution, and recognition looks overdue.
responses.response: Your case is stronger than I judged it in round 1, because the distance and driving-force dependence was measured in defined, engineered metalloproteins, and I regard those structures as sound evidence. I still do not support B009 ahead of B052, for two reasons you raise yourself: the framework rests on Marcus theory, and Dutton and Moser's distance rules and Hopfield's earlier theory fall outside a two-name citation. You also say that you may overweight a field close to your own. In answer to the chair's last question, I could support it as a competitive candidate if the Dutton and Moser priority were resolved, but I do not rank it in my top three today.

uncertainties: Whether Kosugi's tin-amide work was general enough to share credit. I have not checked the original papers, and my judgment relies on memory.
Whether colleagues who rank B052 lower will accept that C-N reductive-elimination control is a new principle and not a sequel to the 2010 prize.
Whether the committee will converge on one prize or split across B052, B002 and B004, and whether any of the latter two can be given a clean three-name credit.
Whether the in vivo evidence for condensates will become strong enough to change my view of B002.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no personal tie to Buchwald, Hartwig or Kosugi and none of the shortlisted candidates is at Stockholm University or in my electron-crystallography field. I am a colleague of the Secretary, Peter Brzezinski, who has declared closeness to B009. That does not affect my view of B009, which I do not rank in my top three.
